title: Who built it, who bought it, who sold it
lede: Roles follow the sources cited in each entry. A later career appears only where a source states it.

people.name: Frank P. Thomas Jr.
people.text: Succeeded his father at the family equipment company, took on the flame broiler, and opened the 1957 pilot stand to demonstrate it.[^5][^6]
people.later: Died in 2007 in Taos, New Mexico, according to a local history.[^9]

people.name: Donald J. Thomas
people.text: Frank’s brother and partner in General Equipment and Burger Chef. The brothers sold to General Foods in 1968.[^6]

people.name: Robert Wildman
people.text: Partner in the first restaurant and an executive of the equipment business. The Encyclopedia of Indianapolis also links him to the Ponderosa and Rax chains.[^5][^7]

people.name: Arthur E. Larkin Jr.
people.text: Retired abruptly in April 1972 at 55, after the write-off. “Burger Chef was the event,” he told the Times.[^1]

people.name: C. W. (Tex) Cook
people.role: Chairman and chief executive, General Foods
people.text: Took back the presidency after Larkin’s departure and oversaw the retreat to a regional chain.[^1]

people.name: James L. Ferguson
people.role: Chairman and chief executive, General Foods, 1981
people.text: Announced the sale, saying the business was not central to the company’s long-term direction.[^3]

people.name: Jack Laughery
people.text: Led the buyer. In November 1982 he expected a combined system of about 2,100 units in 38 states.[^10]

people.name: Jayne Friedt, Ruth Shelton, Daniel Davis and Mark Flemmonds
people.text: The four young staff of the Crawfordsville Road restaurant who were abducted and killed in November 1978. No one has been convicted.[^15][^16]
